newsitem.title: USA: Boeing 747 has good safety record despite crashes.
newsitem.headline: Boeing 747 has good safety record despite crashes.

text.p: In 27 years of service, the 747 jumbo jet of Boeing Co. has established itself as among the safest and most popular airliners in the sky despite its involvement in several major crashes.

Tuesday's crash of Korean Air Lines Flight 801 marked the 18th time a 747 has been destroyed in an accident and the first since last year's still-unexplained explosion and crash of TWA Flight 800 near New York, which killed all 230 people aboard.

But with 1,100 of the jumbo jets in service around the world, the planes have taken off and landed millions of times without incident, resulting in an accident rate of 1.8 for every million departures -- roughly the same as other Western-built planes.

"It's one of the safest airplanes ever built," said Marty Salfen, senior vice president of the International Airline Passengers Association. "If you look at the amount of hours it's flown and the amount of passengers it's flown, it's got a great track record."
That might surprise sceptics who thought the big bird would never fly when Boeing executives developed it in the 1960s and it nearly dragged the company into bankruptcy.

The plane's first delivery in 1970 flew in the teeth of a worldwide recession, and early glitches and production miscues did nothing to improve sales prospects. But the hump-backed four-engine plane eventually caught on and ushered in a new area of affordable transoceanic air travel.
Today the 747 remains one of Boeing's most profitable and lucrative models. There is a backlog of about 150 orders, and the company plans to boost production next year to five a month from four.

At an average list price of $165 million, the plane is Boeing's most expensive, and with a capacity for 416 passengers in the typical three-class configuration of the current 747-400, the jet is by far the world's biggest.

Boeing's European rival, Airbus Industrie, has been planning to develop an even bigger jet dubbed the A3XX, but Boeing executives concluded this year there was not enough demand to justify a new, larger version of the 747.

Inevitably, the 747 has been involved in some of the world's biggest aviation disasters, although many have been caused by deliberate attack, as the distinctive American-built plane has turned out to be an inviting target for saboteurs.

In the best-known incident, a bomb destroyed a Pan Am 747 over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988, killing 270 people. A bomb also was suspected in the 1985 crash of an Air India jet off the Irish coast that killed 329 people.
The 747 was involved in the two biggest aviation disasters -- a 1977 runway collision of two jets that killed 583 people and a 1985 crash that killed 524 -- but both were blamed on human error.

Probably the most serious 747 crash blamed on a design flaw was the 1992 crash of an El Al cargo jet into an Amsterdam apartment building that killed more than 50 people. Boeing later agreed to pay for modifications to strengthen the engine mounts on all 747s in the world fleet.

The cause of the July, 17, 1996, crash of Flight 800 has not been determined, but investigators studying the disaster for the National Transportation Safety Board have urged changes that would prevent fuel-tank explosions like the one the NTSB says was involved in that crash.

As for Korean Air Lines, Salfen, of the passenger association, said it had a relatively high accident rate of 1.91 per million departures over the past 10 years, compared with the worldwide rate of 0.581 per million.
The figure does not include the loss of KAL Flight 007, a Boeing 747 that strayed into Soviet airspace in 1983 and was shot down, resulting in the loss of 269 lives.
